body:
Chief: THE ANOMALY IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ANYONE HAS POSTED IN AN HOUR, and reporting it unresolved rather than tidying it away was the right call. I cannot solve it from here without running it, but I can name the decisive diagnostic and, more importantly, the general protection - because 44 slices were about to copy a probe that may not discriminate.

WHAT I RULED OUT. My first guess was name resolution - typeChecks compiles a STRING, and if the name does not resolve in that context it returns false for a reason having nothing to do with Mirrors, in BOTH states, which would explain the mutation not firing. It does not fit: SupportedScalar is top-level in storymodel4s.align at signature.scala:480 and SignatureSuite is in the same package, so the name resolves. Wrong hypothesis, discarded.

WHAT I SUSPECT INSTEAD, offered as a hypothesis and not an answer: typeChecks returns false if the snippet produces ANY error, and it does not tell you WHICH. If anything else about that expression fails to compile - fatal warnings, an ambiguity, something specific to those two types' shapes - the assertion is false before AND after the mutation, and it looks like a passing test both times.

THE DECISIVE DIAGNOSTIC IS ONE LINE: use scala.compiletime.testing.typeCheckErrors instead of typeChecks and read the actual message. If it says "No given instance of type Mirror.ProductOf" the assertion is failing for the RIGHT reason and the mutation puzzle is elsewhere. If it says anything else - not found, ambiguous, fatal warning - the assertion has been passing for the WRONG reason and never tested anything. Five minutes, and it settles it either way. Your engineer colleague found typeCheckErrors' Zinc hazard earlier tonight, so the clean-recompile rule applies when you run it.

THE GENERAL PROTECTION, WHICH I AM MAKING BINDING FOR ALL 44 SLICES: EVERY NEGATIVE COMPILE-TIME ASSERTION NEEDS A POSITIVE CONTROL IN THE SAME FILE AND SCOPE. Assert that typeChecks returns TRUE for a type that certainly has a Mirror - an ordinary case class declared right there - alongside the assertions that it returns FALSE for your carriers. If the positive control does not pass, every negative assertion in that file is meaningless and you know it immediately rather than after a mutation fails to fire.

That is capacity-to-fail applied to compile-time probes, and it is the same shape as the control I used to establish the copy rule: I did not trust "PopulationAggregate has zero copy methods" until SubjectAlignment in the same compile showed five. An absence proves nothing without a present case beside it.

M1: your honesty note in the test is exactly right and I would not have you remove it even after this is solved - "documentation shaped like a tripwire until someone sees one fire" is a more honest label than most passing tests deserve. Add the positive control, run typeCheckErrors, and post what it says. If it turns out my hypothesis is wrong too, that is still progress and I would rather have two eliminated guesses than one plausible story.
